How much ghosting are we talking about?

For any significant jitter reduction, quite a lot of ghosting. To be fair this is basically the standard TAA trade-off question, it's just rephrased a bit with this method, as it's trying to pick a sample within the current frame as the resolve instead of a combination of a clipped history and input sample which is the typical approach.

Basically the Jitter is a result of the fact the current Frame just doesn't have any samples that are anyhow resembling the history.

The problem is, your task is to determine if you want to instantly switch, or gradually switch to the new value
If you instantly switch, but are wrong, as the content is simply undersampled, you get unwanted jitter.
If you gradually switch, but are wrong, and the content has changed, you get unwanted ghosts.
You simply do not have any way of knowing on a per-pixel level which it is, and your best guess are the pixel's neighbours which will themselves not have all the information either.

Now what ML could do is figure out if the content has changed or is simply undersampled, making significantly better guesses on a case-by-case basis.

I have looked at this naive type TAA as reference (as it's the Holy Grail of AA when the scene is 100% static and you let it converge) and I have observed the inputs in slow motion at lower Integer scaled Resolution, and I'm afraid the problem is History Color clipping simply isn't a good anti-ghosting strategy.

Looking at the same 3x3 pixels Input only where currently there is jitter, the problem becomes somewhat obvious.. Basically I've seen the Jittering edges (in some cases I've looked at) completely changing their Chroma and Intensity (so think one frame they're all some type of red, and the next they're all without any red and just various green intensities), which automatically triggers history to be rejected thus creating jitter, or you have to give it so much tolerance it just fails to do any anti ghosting.

Now maybe moving to YCoCg could lead to better results if you're able to interpret the results better in that color space, which could explain why it's so common in TAA implementations

> Now maybe moving to YCoCg could lead to better results if you're able to interpret the results better in that color space

YCoCg simply means that there's one luminance component (grayscale) and two color components (chroma) per pixel, unlike RGB which uses three primary colors. It might be better than doing comparisons in RGB space, maybe... But if there's issues with detecting jitter/ghosting through color detection, YCoCg won't ever make that go away entirely.

For reference of a good use-case of YCoCg, image/video codecs use YCoCg with full-res luminance and half-res chroma to save space, since the human eye is good at discerning luminance but bad at discerning chroma, so in that context the benefit is obvious. By comparison, the TAA benefit just feels iffy.

Have you looked into other approaches though? Like using depth/normals/glossiness/AO/motion from present or past frames? Comparing history deviation with nearby pixels in a frame to tell apart jitter and ghosting? Anything goes really, so long as it helps to filter out the disocclusion issues.

Sometimes all that is required is handling things from a different Perspective, so YCoCg could do much more then it seems.

I have been unable to get anything besides depth and motion vectors.

Depth however doesn't work when I cannot get the Camera Projections to load up so it's meaningless without them.
Also, much like the color can be inconsistent, all the other buffers also suffer the same problem when they are under sampled.

Also all the methods I tried to detect if there is instability have resulted in ghosting (I even had FSR 2 Pixel Locking type artifact in one of the attempts)

Suffice to say however the more I study the problems the more clear it is to me as to why FSR 2-3 and TAAU and TSR have such serious Ghosting problems when Upscaling (since upscaling just makes this problem worse) and why FSR 4 and DLSS 4 do a significantly better job at that, as there doesn't seem like there is an Algorithmic solution that covers all the bases, and you just have to learn where there is a problem and clean it up on a case by case basis.

Hmm, Interesting discovery... despite using ONLY using the input frame for picking resolve color (and doing so within a 3x3 kernel), and having the history only act as a guide to where in that input kernel you pick your resolve sample from (so no blending history with the input) there are still some instances where you can get fairly significant Ghosting.

This means several things...
1) No form of Color Clipping will EVER resolve ghosting completely, and the current heavy reliance on it doing the Heavy Lifting is why it fails so much.
2) TAA should be developed with No Color Clipping enabled, and full Focus has to be on Alternative Anti-Ghosting Methods (such as Figuring out the most effective Disocclusion criteria) and the Color Clipping Best case scenario can be used as a Last ditch Crutch where you cannot get all the relevant information (say in case of Alpha Transparencies)
3) Significant additional Frame Information is required to deal with ghosts, as the Color is not a valid Analytical test, meaning you need to actually be aware of what content is rendered from frame to frame, and what changes occur to the content. This is Information Godot does not currently provide as far as I know (such as object IDs, object Transforms over time, 3D motion vectors etc)
